title: Why "I scratched my own itch" isn't enough: seven implied claims founders must test
summary: Jason Cohen argues that the common "I had the problem myself" origin story hides seven assumptions, several false, which explains why most such startups fail. Treat your own problem as a spark and a starting theory, then interview real customers, validate the market, and build the non-code skills a company needs.

principles.text: "I had the problem myself" implies seven claims; some are true, which blinds you to the false ones.
principles.quote: Because some are true, you can't see why some are false.

principles.text: You are not your customer; you built your own solution out of frustration, so you resemble none of the buyers.
principles.quote: You are absolutely not like your customers.

principles.text: Treat your own experience as a theory to test through customer interviews, not as proof you understand the market.
principles.quote: Treat this initial understanding as a starting point rather than the end-point, and interview customers purposefully to get the full answer.

principles.text: The biggest failure is assuming others share the problem and will pay; many conditions must hold for a market to exist.
principles.quote: There have to be enough people who have the problem, and know they have the problem so that they're out searching for a solution, and have a budget for solving it, and would rather buy from you than a competitor, and will stick around for longer than a couple of months.

principles.text: A real problem does not imply a market; legitimate problems vastly outnumber markets willing to buy solutions.
principles.quote: There are a hundred times more legitimate problems in the world than there are markets to buy solutions to those problems.

principles.text: Executing the company means marketing, hooks, leads and interviews, not writing code. Don't retreat into coding.
principles.quote: But "it" isn't the code. "It" is everything else a company must do to succeed.
